title: Volumes
summary: Give containers shared and longer-lived files: emptyDir, hostPath, configMap/secret/projected, subPath and CSI.

sections.heading: Why volumes, and how they plug in

blocks.text: When a container crashes, it restarts empty, and containers in a bay can't easily share files. The fix is a **locker attached to the bay** (a volume). Some lockers vanish with the bay; others outlast it. Either way, contents survive container restarts. List lockers once (`.spec.volumes`); each container mounts them where it likes (`volumeMounts`).
Files written inside a container are lost when it crashes: the kubelet restarts it with a **clean state**. Containers in one Pod also have no easy way to share files. Volumes fix both.

items: **Ephemeral** volume types live and die with the Pod. **Persistent** volumes outlive any single Pod.
Whatever the type, data in a Pod's volumes survives **container restarts**.
Declare volumes once in `.spec.volumes`, then mount them per container in `.spec.containers[*].volumeMounts`.
For each container, you specify independently where to mount each volume it uses.
A volume can't be mounted inside another volume (use `subPath` instead), and can't hard-link into another volume.

blocks.text: A Pod can use **any number** of volume types at once.

sections.heading: emptyDir: scratch space shared by the Pod

blocks.text: An `emptyDir` locker appears **empty** when the bay lands on a ship, shared by every container in the bay. It survives container crashes, but when the bay leaves the ship, its contents are gone for good. `medium: Memory` makes a fast RAM locker that counts against the writer's memory limit; `sizeLimit` caps it.

An `emptyDir` is created **empty** when the Pod is assigned to a node. All containers in the Pod can read and write it, at the same or different paths. When the Pod leaves the node for any reason, the data is **deleted permanently**. A container crash does not remove the Pod, so the data survives crashes.

items: Typical uses: scratch space for a disk-based merge sort, checkpoints of a long computation, files fetched by one container and served by another.
By default it sits on whatever backs the node (disk, SSD, network storage).
`medium: Memory` mounts a **tmpfs** instead. It is fast, but written files count against the writing container's **memory limit**.
`sizeLimit` caps the volume. With no size set, a memory-backed volume is sized to node allocatable memory.

blocks.text:
volumes:
- name: cache-volume
  emptyDir:
    sizeLimit: 500Mi
    medium: Memory   # optional: RAM-backed
To share files between two containers in one Pod, define one `emptyDir` under `volumes` and add a `volumeMounts` entry with the same `name` to **each** container.

A `hostPath` locker is a hatch into the **ship's own hold**. It is risky: the hold may contain keys enabling container escape, and identical bays act differently on different ships. Avoid it when you can. Fair uses: reading `/var/log` read-only, or a config file for a static bay. Its `type` says what must already exist.
`hostPath` mounts a file or directory from the **node** into the Pod. Few Pods need it, and the docs say to avoid it when you can, for example by using a `local` PersistentVolume instead.

items: It can expose privileged credentials or APIs (such as the container runtime socket) that enable **container escape**.
Identical Pods may behave differently on different nodes because the node files differ.
Its usage isn't counted as ephemeral storage, so heavy use can cause **disk pressure**.
Admission rules restricting host directories only work if those mounts are also forced **read only**.
Legitimate uses: a log shipper reading `/var/log` read-only; giving a **static Pod** a config file (static Pods can't use ConfigMaps).

rows: Creates an empty directory (0755) if nothing is there
Creates an empty file (0644); does **not** create the parent directory
A file / UNIX socket must exist
A device must exist (Linux nodes only)

blocks.text:
volumes:
- name: <volume-name>
  hostPath:
    path: <host-path>
    type: Directory   # optional

Some lockers come pre-stocked: the bay's instruction sheet (ConfigMap) or sealed envelope (Secret) appears as files. The sheet or envelope must **exist first**, and the locker is always read-only. Secret lockers sit in memory (tmpfs), never on disk. Use `items` to choose file names. Caution: a container mounting one through `subPath` never sees later updates.
These volumes turn API data into files. Name the object in the volume; optionally use `items` to map a `key` to a file `path` under the mount point.

volumes:
- name: config-vol
  configMap:
    name: <configmap-name>
    items:
    - key: <key>
      path: <file-name>   # appears at <mountPath>/<file-name>

items: The ConfigMap or Secret must **exist before** the Pod can use it.
Both are **always mounted readOnly**.
`secret` volumes are backed by **tmpfs**, so secrets are never written to non-volatile storage.
Text is exposed as UTF-8 files; use `binaryData` for other encodings.

blocks.text: A container that mounts a ConfigMap, Secret or downwardAPI volume through `subPath` will **not** receive updates when the source changes.

A `projected` locker gathers several deliveries into **one shelf**: an instruction sheet, a sealed envelope, a robot crew badge token (`serviceAccountToken`) and more. All must come from the bay's own company yard. A badge token lasts one hour by default, and at least 600 seconds. As usual, a `subPath` mount sees no updates.

A `projected` volume merges several sources into **one directory**. Allowed sources: `secret`, `downwardAPI`, `configMap`, `serviceAccountToken`, `clusterTrustBundle` and `podCertificate`. Every source must be in the **same namespace** as the Pod.

volumes:
- name: all-in-one
  projected:
    sources:
    - secret:
        name: <secret-name>
    - configMap:
        name: <configmap-name>
    - serviceAccountToken:
        path: token
        expirationSeconds: 3600

items: A projected secret uses `name` (not `secretName`), matching ConfigMap naming.
`defaultMode` can only be set at the projected level; set `mode` per item if needed.
`serviceAccountToken`: `audience` defaults to the API server's identifier; `expirationSeconds` defaults to **1 hour** and must be at least **600** seconds.
As with other sources, a `subPath` mount of a projected volume gets no updates.

blocks.text: One big locker can be split into labelled drawers with `subPath`, so a database and a web server each use their own folder of the same locker. `subPathExpr` names the drawer from an environment variable, like the bay's name, but you can't use both. `readOnly: true` locks the drawer for that container only.

`volumeMounts[*].subPath` mounts a sub-path of the volume instead of its root, so one volume can serve several mounts. For example, a database and a web server can each mount their own folder of one PVC.

volumeMounts:
- name: site-data
  mountPath: /var/lib/mysql
  subPath: mysql
- name: workdir1
  mountPath: /logs
  subPathExpr: $(POD_NAME)   # round brackets

items: `subPathExpr` builds the sub-path from downward API **environment variables**. It and `subPath` are **mutually exclusive**.
`readOnly: true` on a mount stops that container writing; other containers may still mount the same volume read-write.
Linux read-only mounts don't cover **sub-mounts** underneath by default; set `recursiveReadOnly` to change that.

blocks.text: Some lockers are listed right on the bay's paperwork and come and go with it. The cargo officer (kubelet) runs the simple ones. A **generic ephemeral** locker instead files a real warehouse rental request (PVC) named after the bay, which the bay owns, so it is removed with the bay. Quota still applies.
Ephemeral volumes are declared **inline** in the Pod spec and are created and deleted with the Pod.

items: `emptyDir`, `configMap`, `downwardAPI`, `secret`: local ephemeral storage managed by the **kubelet**.
`image`: mounts files from a container image or artifact.
**CSI ephemeral volumes**: inline `csi` volumes from third-party drivers that support them.

**Generic ephemeral volumes** (an `ephemeral` volume with a `volumeClaimTemplate`): work with any driver that supports dynamic provisioning, and can offer a fixed size, snapshots, cloning and resizing.

blocks.text: For a generic ephemeral volume, a controller creates a real PVC named `<pod-name>-<volume-name>` in the Pod's namespace. The Pod **owns** it, so the PVC is garbage-collected when the Pod is deleted. `WaitForFirstConsumer` binding is recommended for these volumes.
Users who can create Pods can create PVCs indirectly through generic ephemeral volumes. Namespace PVC quota still applies.

Locker types were once built into the port itself (in-tree). Now a standard **warehouse plug** (CSI) lets vendors ship drivers separately. With a driver installed, a bay can use it through a rental request (PVC), a generic ephemeral locker, or an inline CSI locker. Many old built-in types now redirect to CSI.

Volume plugins used to be **in-tree**: compiled and shipped inside Kubernetes. **CSI** (Container Storage Interface) and the deprecated **FlexVolume** are out-of-tree, so vendors can ship drivers without touching the Kubernetes code base.

items: CSI is the standard interface orchestrators use to expose arbitrary storage systems to containers.
Once a CSI driver is deployed, a Pod can use it three ways: through a **PersistentVolumeClaim**, a **generic ephemeral volume**, or a **CSI ephemeral volume** (if the driver supports it).
Key fields on a CSI PersistentVolume: `driver` (driver name) and `volumeHandle` (unique volume ID).
Many old in-tree types (for example `portworxVolume`) are deprecated and redirected to CSI drivers.

flashcards.front: What happens to a container's own files when it crashes?
flashcards.back: They are lost. The kubelet restarts the container with a clean state; volumes keep data across container restarts.

flashcards.front: Where do you declare volumes vs. mount them?
flashcards.back: Declare in `.spec.volumes`; mount per container in `.spec.containers[*].volumeMounts`.

flashcards.front: When is an emptyDir created and when is its data deleted?
flashcards.back: Created empty when the Pod is assigned to a node; deleted permanently when the Pod is removed from the node. It survives container crashes.
Mounts a RAM-backed tmpfs. Files written count against the container's memory limit.
Exposing privileged credentials/APIs (container escape), different behaviour per node, and unmonitored disk usage causing disk pressure.

flashcards.front: Which hostPath `type` creates a missing directory, and with what permissions?
Are ConfigMap and Secret volumes writable?
flashcards.back: No. They are always mounted readOnly. Secret volumes are tmpfs-backed.

flashcards.front: Why might a mounted ConfigMap file never change after an update?
flashcards.back: The container mounts it with `subPath`; subPath mounts don't receive updates.

flashcards.front: Which sources can a projected volume combine?
flashcards.back: secret, downwardAPI, configMap, serviceAccountToken, clusterTrustBundle, podCertificate — all from the Pod's namespace.
`subPath` is a fixed sub-path of the volume; `subPathExpr` expands downward API env vars like `$(POD_NAME)`. They're mutually exclusive.

flashcards.front: What PVC name does a generic ephemeral volume get?
flashcards.back: `<pod-name>-<volume-name>`, owned by the Pod and deleted with it.

flashcards.front: Three ways a Pod can use a CSI driver?
flashcards.back: Via a PersistentVolumeClaim, a generic ephemeral volume, or a CSI ephemeral volume (if supported).

questions.stem: Two containers in the same Pod must exchange files, and the data can be thrown away when the Pod goes. Which volume fits best?

options.explanation: An emptyDir is shared by all containers in the Pod and lives as long as the Pod is on the node.
hostPath exposes the node filesystem and carries security risks; it isn't needed for Pod-local sharing.
Works, but it's durable storage that outlives the Pod — more than this need.
Secret volumes are always read-only and carry API data, not scratch files.

questions.stem: True or false: If a container in a Pod crashes and is restarted, data it wrote to an emptyDir volume is lost.

options.explanation: A container crash doesn't remove the Pod from the node, so emptyDir data survives.
Correct. emptyDir data is only deleted when the Pod is removed from the node.

questions.stem: A Pod sets `emptyDir.medium: Memory`. Which statement is true?

options.text: Files written to it count against the writing container's memory limit
options.explanation: tmpfs is RAM-backed, so its usage counts toward the memory limit.
Any emptyDir is deleted permanently when the Pod leaves the node.

options.text: It is stored on the node's root disk
options.explanation: That's the default medium; Memory uses tmpfs.

options.text: sizeLimit cannot be used with it
options.explanation: The docs' example sets sizeLimit together with medium: Memory.

questions.stem: Which are documented risks of hostPath volumes? Select 3.

options.text: They can expose privileged APIs such as the container runtime socket
options.explanation: This can lead to container escape.

options.text: Identical Pods may behave differently on different nodes
options.explanation: Node files can differ.

options.text: Usage isn't counted as ephemeral storage, so it can cause disk pressure
options.explanation: You have to monitor it yourself.

options.text: They are always deleted when the Pod is deleted
options.explanation: hostPath data lives on the node; it isn't removed with the Pod.

options.text: They can only be mounted read-only
options.explanation: They can be mounted read-write, which is part of the danger.

questions.stem: A hostPath volume uses `type: FileOrCreate` for `/var/local/aaa/1.txt`, but `/var/local/aaa` doesn't exist on the node. What happens?

options.text: The Pod fails to start, because FileOrCreate doesn't create the parent directory
options.explanation: Mount the directory separately (e.g. DirectoryOrCreate) as the docs' example shows.

options.text: The kubelet creates both the directory and the file
options.explanation: Only the file is created; the parent must already exist.

options.text: The volume silently mounts an empty directory instead
options.explanation: There's no such fallback.

options.text: Nothing is checked, as with the empty-string type
options.explanation: The empty string skips checks; FileOrCreate doesn't.

questions.stem: You update a ConfigMap. One container mounts the whole volume, another mounts a single key with `subPath`. What do they see?

options.text: Only the container without subPath receives the update
options.explanation: subPath mounts of a ConfigMap don't receive updates.
The subPath mount won't.

options.text: Neither sees updates until the Pod restarts
options.explanation: The full-volume mount does receive updates.
It just keeps the old content.

questions.stem: True or false: Secret volumes are backed by tmpfs, so their contents are never written to non-volatile storage.

options.explanation: Correct — that's how the volumes page describes secret volumes.
They are tmpfs-backed, RAM only.

questions.stem: Which are valid sources inside a `projected` volume? Select 3.

options.explanation: Listed as a projectable source.
Listed.
Listed.
PVCs aren't a projected source; mount them as a separate volume.
Not a projected source.

questions.stem: In a projected volume you want the secret files to have a non-default mode. Where can you set it?

options.text: `defaultMode` on the projected volume, or `mode` on an individual item
options.explanation: defaultMode only exists at the projected level; per-item mode is allowed.
defaultMode can't be set per source in a projection.

options.text: Only in the Secret object itself
options.explanation: Modes are set in the Pod's volume definition.

options.text: Modes can't be changed for projected volumes
options.explanation: The docs show `mode: 0777` on an item.
The value must be at least 10 minutes.
3600 (1 hour) is the default, not a requirement.
It is; it sets the token's expected validity.
serviceAccountToken is a projected source.

questions.stem: Several Pods log to one hostPath directory, and each Pod should write to its own sub-directory named after the Pod. Which mount field does this?

options.text: `subPathExpr: $(POD_NAME)` with POD_NAME from the downward API
options.explanation: subPathExpr expands env vars from the downward API.
subPath is literal, and expansion uses round brackets in subPathExpr.
That controls how mounts propagate, not the sub-directory name.
That only blocks writes.

questions.stem: A Pod named `web` has a generic ephemeral volume named `cache`. What happens to the PVC it creates?

options.text: A PVC named `web-cache` is created; it's owned by the Pod and deleted with it
options.explanation: Names are `<pod>-<volume>` and the Pod owns the PVC.

options.text: A PVC named `cache` is created and kept after the Pod is deleted
options.explanation: The name includes the Pod name and the PVC is garbage-collected.

options.text: No PVC is created; the kubelet manages it like emptyDir
options.explanation: Generic ephemeral volumes create a real PVC.

options.text: You must create the PVC first
options.explanation: The ephemeral volume controller creates it.

questions.stem: True or false: CSI lets storage vendors ship volume plugins without adding code to the Kubernetes repository.

options.explanation: Correct — CSI (and the deprecated FlexVolume) are out-of-tree plugin mechanisms.
That's exactly the purpose of out-of-tree plugins.

questions.stem: Through which mechanisms can a Pod use volumes from a CSI driver? Select 3.

options.explanation: The common path.
Listed.

options.text: A CSI ephemeral volume, if the driver supports it
options.explanation: Listed, with that condition.
Projected volumes combine secret/configMap/downwardAPI/token-type sources, not CSI.
That mounts a node device, not a CSI volume.
